title: Common Diseases and Healthy Living
summary: Causes, symptoms, prevention and treatment of common diseases (TB, diabetes, hypertension, epilepsy and obesity), eating disorders, where to get help, and healthy eating and lifestyle choices.

notes.text: A disease that **spreads** from person to person, caused by germs such as bacteria or viruses. Examples: TB, flu, HIV, COVID-19.
A disease that **cannot be caught** from someone else. It is often linked to lifestyle, genes or age. Examples: diabetes, high blood pressure, heart disease, epilepsy.

rows: Tuberculosis (TB)
Bacteria spread through the air when an infected person coughs or sneezes. Spreads easily in crowded, poorly ventilated rooms.
Cough for more than two weeks, coughing up blood, night sweats, weight loss, fever, tiredness
Open windows, cover coughs. TB is **curable** with free clinic treatment, but the full 6-month course of pills must be finished.
Diabetes (type 2)
The body cannot use **insulin** properly, so blood sugar stays too high. Linked to being overweight, inactivity and family history.
Thirst, passing urine often, tiredness, blurred vision, slow-healing sores
Healthy eating, less sugar, exercise, keeping a healthy weight. Treated with diet, tablets or insulin.
Hypertension (high blood pressure)
Blood pushes too hard against the artery walls. Linked to salt, stress, smoking, alcohol, being overweight and family history.
Often **no symptoms** (the 'silent killer'); sometimes headaches or dizziness
Less salt, exercise, no smoking, regular check-ups. Treated with daily medication; can cause strokes and heart attacks if untreated.
Epilepsy
A condition of the brain that causes **seizures** (fits). It is **not** contagious and is not caused by witchcraft.
Seizures: jerking movements, staring spells, loss of consciousness
Cannot be prevented, but medication controls seizures in most people. People with epilepsy can study, work and live normally.
Obesity
Taking in more energy (food) than the body uses over a long time. Linked to fast food, sugary drinks and lack of exercise.
Very high body weight for one's height; tiredness and joint pain
Balanced meals, smaller portions, fewer sugary drinks, daily physical activity.

notes.title: Worked example 1: helping someone having a seizure
notes.problem: A classmate falls to the floor and starts jerking. What should you do, and what should you NOT do?
steps: Stay calm and keep other learners back. Note the time the seizure started.
Move hard or sharp objects away and put something soft under the person's head.
Do NOT hold them down and do NOT put anything in their mouth.
When the jerking stops, roll them onto their side (recovery position) and stay with them.
Call a teacher; call an ambulance if it lasts longer than 5 minutes or they are injured.
notes.answer: Protect them from injury, time the seizure, turn them on their side afterwards and get help. Never restrain them or put anything in their mouth.

rows: Anorexia nervosa
Extreme fear of gaining weight; the person starves themselves.
Very thin but believes they are fat, skips meals, over-exercises, loses periods
Bulimia nervosa
Cycles of **binge eating** followed by **purging** (vomiting, laxatives) or extreme exercise.
Disappears to the bathroom after meals, damaged teeth, sore throat, secretive eating
Binge-eating disorder
Often eating very large amounts while feeling out of control, without purging.
Eating when not hungry, eating alone, guilt and shame afterwards

notes.text: Eating disorders are **serious mental illnesses**, not choices or phases. They are linked to low self-esteem, pressure from media and social media to look a certain way, stress and a need for control. They can damage the heart, bones and other organs. Recovery is possible with help from a doctor, psychologist and dietician.

notes.label: Where to get help
notes.text: Talk to a trusted adult, a teacher, the school nurse or your local clinic. You can also call the SADAG mental health helpline on 0800 567 567 or the Childline on 116 (both free).

notes.caption: A healthy plate: half vegetables and fruit, a quarter starch (preferably wholegrain) and a quarter protein, with water to drink and little sugar, salt and fat.

items: Eat breakfast; it gives you energy and helps you concentrate at school.
Choose water instead of fizzy drinks. A 500 mℓ cooldrink can contain about 13 teaspoons of sugar.
Be active for at least **60 minutes a day**: walk, play sport, dance.
Sleep 8 to 10 hours a night, and avoid smoking, vaping and alcohol.
Go for check-ups: clinics test for TB, diabetes and high blood pressure for free.

notes.title: Worked example 2: improving a lunch box
notes.problem: Musa's daily lunch is a white-bread polony sandwich, a packet of chips and a 500 mℓ fizzy drink. Suggest three changes and explain why.
steps: Swap the fizzy drink for water: cuts about 13 teaspoons of sugar, lowering the risk of obesity, diabetes and tooth decay.
Swap chips for a fruit (banana, apple): adds vitamins and fibre and cuts salt and fat.
Use brown or wholegrain bread with egg, peanut butter or chicken: more fibre and better protein, less processed meat and salt.
notes.answer: Water instead of a fizzy drink, fruit instead of chips, and wholegrain bread with a healthier protein filling.

options: the air, when an infected person coughs

Which disease is called the 'silent killer' because it often has no symptoms?

questions.explanation: Epilepsy is a brain condition. It is not contagious.

options: Put something soft under their head
Put a spoon in their mouth

questions.prompt: Match each eating disorder or disease to its description.

pairs.right: Starving oneself from a fear of gaining weight
Excess body weight from taking in more energy than is used

questions.prompt: On a healthy plate, how much should be vegetables and fruit?
Name THREE lifestyle habits that increase a person's risk of developing diabetes or high blood pressure, and suggest a healthier alternative for each.
questions.memo:
Any three habits with alternatives (1 + 1 each):
✓ eating a lot of sugar / drinking fizzy drinks → drink water, choose fruit
✓ eating salty, fried or processed food → cook with less salt, grill or boil
✓ lack of exercise → be active for 60 minutes a day
✓ smoking → quit, seek help
✓ drinking alcohol → avoid or limit
✓ stress → relaxation, talking to someone, enough sleep

questions.prompt: You notice that a friend skips lunch every day, has lost a lot of weight and says she is 'too fat'. Explain what this might be and describe how you could help her.
questions.memo:
✓ identifies possible anorexia / an eating disorder (1)
✓ talk to her privately and kindly, without blaming or judging (1)
✓ encourage her to speak to a trusted adult, school nurse, counsellor or clinic / SADAG (1)
✓ tell a trusted adult yourself if she will not, because it can be life-threatening; avoid comments about weight (1)
